name: Fired Pottery
description: Clay fired hot enough to hold liquids and survive a furnace

name: Copper Smelting
description: Roast copper ore and reduce it with charcoal in a clay furnace; tin ore smelts the same way

name: Lime Burning
description: Heat limestone to 900 °C to make quicklime and slaked lime

name: Bronze Alloying
description: Melt copper with about one tenth tin for a harder metal

name: Iron Smelting
description: Reduce iron ore in a charcoal bloomery and hammer out the slag

name: Bellows
description: Forced air lets furnaces pass 1200 °C

name: Salt Evaporation
description: Dry seawater in shallow pans for common salt; the bitter liquor left is bittern

name: Fermentation
description: Yeast turns sugar into ethanol in a barrel; in an open vat it sours into vinegar

name: Leavened Bread
description: Sugar-fed dough rises into bread that restores more hunger than vanilla bread

name: Glassmaking
description: Melt sand with twice its weight of wood ash into forest glass

name: Writing and Ink
description: Soot ink on paper; lets you write treatises

name: Leather Tanning
description: Soak hides in water with oak bark to make leather

name: Cupellation
description: Roast silver-bearing galena on a bone-ash cupel: the lead soaks in as litharge and silver is left

name: Mercury from Cinnabar
description: Roast cinnabar to drive off mercury vapour and condense it

name: Bronze Tools and Weapons
description: Bronze tools, weapons and armor: better than stone, close to iron

name: Iron Tools and Weapons
description: Wrought iron tools and armor, tougher than vanilla iron (they replace its recipes)

name: Lead Smelting
description: Roast galena to litharge and reduce it with charcoal to lead

name: Green Vitriol
description: Roast pyrite gently in a lime kiln (under 650 °C) for green vitriol

name: Alembic Distillation
description: Boil and condense liquids to purify them; distils wood into wood alcohol and vinegar

name: Desalination
description: Boil seawater in a copper still and condense the steam: pure fresh water at sea (Richard Hawkins 1594)

name: Mineral Acids
description: Distil green vitriol and saltpetre into sulfuric and nitric acids; salt and acid give hydrochloric acid

name: Saltpetre Refining
description: Leach nitre beds and recrystallise potassium nitrate

name: Blast Furnace
description: A tall furnace that melts iron fully for casting

name: Black Powder
description: Saltpetre with charcoal and sulfur

name: Aqua Regia
description: Nitric plus hydrochloric acid dissolves gold for purification

name: Zinc Distillation
description: Reduce zinc ore in a closed retort and condense the metal; makes brass

name: Printing Press
description: Movable type of lead-tin-antimony alloy; lets you print treatises

name: Iron-Gall Ink
description: Permanent ink from oak galls and green vitriol

name: Porcelain
description: Kaolin fired at 1300 °C into hard white crucibles and labware

name: Ground Lenses
description: A magnifying lens shows what the block you look at is made of

name: Phosphorus
description: Distil phosphorus from bone ash or urine residue

name: Mercury Amalgamation
description: Extract silver from ore with mercury

name: Cementation Steel
description: Pack wrought iron in charcoal for days to make blister steel for tools and armor

name: White Arsenic
description: Roast arsenopyrite in a reverberatory furnace, catch the white arsenic and reduce it with charcoal (Albertus Magnus)

name: Antimony
description: Roast stibnite to its oxide and reduce it with charcoal (Biringuccio, 1540)

name: Bismuth
description: Bismuth melts at 271 °C and runs out of Saxon cobalt ore

name: Cobalt
description: Brandt shows that the blue of cobalt glass comes from a new metal: roast cobaltite and reduce the oxide

name: Coke
description: Bake coal into coke: a fuel hot enough to melt steel

name: Crucible Steel
description: Melt blister steel in a closed crucible at 1600 °C for even steel; the best blades before electricity

name: Steam Engine
description: A coal-fired engine that drives blowing cylinders: furnaces next to it burn 200 °C hotter

name: Pneumatic Chemistry
description: Collect gases under water: hydrogen from iron and acid; oxygen and nitrogen from red-hot saltpetre

name: Voltaic Pile
description: Discs of zinc and copper in brine or acid: the first steady electric current

name: Electrolysis
description: Split molten salts and water with current: sodium

name: Lead Chamber Process
description: Burn sulfur or pyrite into a lead room with steam: sulfuric acid by the barrel

name: Alkaline Earth Metals
description: Calcium, magnesium, barium and strontium by electrolysis of their earths and of bittern

name: Acid Digestion
description: Dissolve ores in hot acid in porcelain-lined vats; borax gives boric acid

name: Lithium
description: Leach spodumene for lithium chloride and electrolyse it (Arfwedson; Bunsen)

name: Boron
description: Strip the oxygen from boric acid with potassium in a sealed crucible

name: Beryllium
description: Chlorinate beryl and reduce the chloride with potassium (Wohler)

name: Selenium
description: Distil selenium out of lead-chamber sludge (Berzelius)

name: Bromine
description: Free bromine from bittern with chlorine (Balard)

name: Iodine
description: Violet vapour from kelp ash and oil of vitriol (Courtois)

name: Cadmium
description: Catch the cadmium that distils from zinc ore before the zinc (Stromeyer)

name: Platinum
description: Dissolve platinum grains from gold ore in aqua regia and press the sponge (Wollaston)

name: Uranium Oxide
description: Roast pitchblende for the black oxide Klaproth named uranium

name: Flintlock Musket
description: A steel-barrelled musket fired by flint: harder hitting and quicker to reload than the hand cannon

name: Dynamo
description: A self-exciting dynamo driven by a steam engine: current by the kilowatt, carried on copper wire (Siemens 1866)

name: Bessemer Converter
description: Blow air through molten pig iron: its own carbon burns and keeps it molten; steel by the tonne

name: Chlor-Alkali Process
description: Electrolyse brine over a mercury cathode: lye, chlorine and hydrogen (Castner and Kellner)

name: Liquid Air
description: Compress and cool air until it is liquid, then boil off nitrogen, argon and oxygen in turn (Linde)

name: Spectroscopy
description: Every element colours a flame with its own lines: a prism finds traces no balance can (Bunsen and Kirchhoff)

name: Electrolytic Refining
description: Refine copper by current; the slime under the anodes holds the precious metals and tellurium

name: Hall-Heroult Process
description: Dissolve alumina in molten cryolite and split it with current: aluminium becomes cheaper than silver

name: Neon, Krypton and Xenon
description: Boil liquid air slowly and read each fraction in the spectroscope (Ramsay and Travers)

name: Caesium and Rubidium
description: The first elements found by spectrum: in the lithium liquor of pegmatite

name: Indium
description: An indigo line in zinc ore: catch indium in the retort flue dust

name: Germanium
description: Mendeleev's eka-silicon, found where he said it would be; reduce its oxide with hydrogen (Winkler)

name: Thallium
description: A bright green line in lead-chamber sludge (Crookes)

name: Platinum Group Metals
description: Part anode slime with aqua regia into platinum, palladium and rhodium; the black residue holds ruthenium, osmium and iridium

name: Bayer Process
description: Dissolve the alumina out of bauxite with hot lye under pressure and leave the iron behind as red mud

name: Gallium
description: Draw gallium from the Bayer liquor: a metal that melts in your hand

name: Fluorine
description: Hydrogen fluoride from fluorspar, electrolysed in platinum: the most reactive element, isolated at last (Moissan)

name: Manganese Steel
description: Ferromanganese from pyrolusite; steel with 12% manganese grows harder where it is struck (Hadfield)

name: Solvay Process
description: Soda ash from salt and limestone with ammonia as the go-between

name: Tungsten Steel
description: Tungsten from wolframite; Mushet's tungsten steel holds its edge when red hot

name: Vanadium
description: Vanadium oxide from vanadinite; reduce it with burning aluminium (Roscoe; Goldschmidt)

name: Contact Process
description: Sulfur dioxide over a hot catalyst: strong sulfuric acid by the tonne

name: Mond Process
description: Carbon monoxide carries nickel off as a gas and lays it down pure (Mond)

name: Radioactivity
description: Uranium salts discharge a gold-leaf electroscope through paper: invisible rays (Becquerel)

name: Helium
description: The gas from uranium ore shows the yellow line seen only in the sun (Ramsay)

name: Radium
description: Follow the activity through tonnes of pitchblende residue to a gram of radium (Marie and Pierre Curie)

name: Polonium
description: The first element found by its radioactivity; named for Poland

name: Actinium
description: Debierne's ray-giving element from the rare-earth part of the residue

name: Radon
description: Radium gives off a radioactive gas: pump it off and seal it in gold seeds (Dorn)

name: Helium from Radium
description: Radium sealed in a tube slowly fills it with helium: alpha rays are helium (Ramsay and Soddy, Rutherford)

name: Thorium
description: Thorium from the black sand of beaches: dissolve its oxide and reduce the chloride with potassium (Berzelius)

name: Smokeless Powder
description: Guncotton gelled into a powder that burns without smoke and three times as strong (Vieille)

name: Breech-Loading Rifle
description: A steel rifle loaded from the back with brass cartridges of smokeless powder (Lebel)

name: Electric Arc Furnace
description: Strike an arc between graphite electrodes: heat no fuel can give, for silicon and ferroalloys (Heroult 1900)

name: Haber-Bosch Process
description: Bread from air: ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen at 200 atmospheres (Haber 1909, Bosch 1913)

name: Froth Flotation
description: Pine oil and bubbles float sulfide grains away from the rock: ores too poor to smelt become worth mining

name: Stainless Steel
description: Steel with an eighth chromium does not rust (Brearley 1913)

name: Rare Earths
description: Crack monazite in acid and crystallize its salts again and again until the rare earths part (Auer von Welsbach)

name: Crystal Bar Process
description: Grow pure zirconium on a hot wire from its iodide vapour (van Arkel and de Boer 1925)

name: Ostwald Process
description: Burn ammonia on a platinum-rhodium gauze: nitric acid without saltpetre

name: Chromium
description: Pure chromium from chromite: roast with soda and burn the green oxide with aluminium (Goldschmidt 1898)

name: Molybdenum
description: Roast molybdenite to its white oxide and reduce it with hydrogen (Hjelm 1781)

name: Rhenium
description: The last stable element found, in the flue of a molybdenite roaster (Noddack, Tacke and Berg 1925)

name: High-Speed Steel
description: Tool steel hardened from near melting cuts while red hot (Taylor and White 1900)

name: Cemented Carbide
description: Tungsten carbide grains sintered in cobalt: wie Diamant (Widia 1926)

name: Beryllium Copper
description: Copper with 2% beryllium is as hard as steel and never sparks: tools for mines and powder works

name: Niobium
description: Niobium parted from tantalum by crystallizing their fluoride salts (Marignac 1866)

name: Tantalum
description: Ductile tantalum melted in the arc for lamp filaments (von Bolton 1903)

name: Lanthanum
description: "Hidden": the earth hiding in ceria (Mosander 1839)

name: Praseodymium and Neodymium
description: Didymium is two elements: green and pink salts after a hundred crystallizations (Auer von Welsbach 1885)

name: Hafnium
description: X-ray lines showed a new element in every zircon; its fluoride crystallizes apart (Coster and Hevesy 1923)

name: Protactinium
description: The mother of actinium, found in pitchblende residue (Hahn and Meitner 1918)

name: Francium
description: Element 87: a branch in actinium's decay, carried by caesium salt, gone within the hour (Perey 1939)

name: Geiger Counter
description: A gas tube that clicks for every ray: read radiation as you walk (Geiger and Muller 1928)

name: Kroll Process
description: Chlorinate the black sand, then strip the chlorine with magnesium under argon: titanium by the tonne (Kroll 1940)

name: Ion Exchange
description: Resin columns part in days the rare earths a century of crystallizing could not (Spedding 1947)

name: Single Crystals
description: Grow one flawless crystal from the melt and sweep it clean: the stuff of transistors (Teal, Pfann)

name: Synthetic Diamond
description: Graphite in molten nickel squeezed to 50000 atmospheres becomes diamond (General Electric 1954)

name: Uranium Metal
description: Green salt reduced by magnesium in a sealed bomb: uranium for the first reactor (Ames 1942)

name: Titanium Alloy
description: Titanium with 6% aluminium and 4% vanadium: netherite's strength, half the weight

name: Scandium
description: Mendeleev's eka-boron, first made as metal in 1937 (Fischer)

name: Samarium and Europium
description: Samarium from samarskite (Lecoq 1879) and europium split from it (Demarcay 1901)

name: Gadolinium and Terbium
description: Gadolinium (Marignac 1880) and terbium, the second earth of Ytterby

name: Dysprosium and Holmium
description: Dysprosium, "hard to get at" (Lecoq 1886), and holmium for Stockholm (Cleve 1878)

name: Erbium and Thulium
description: Pink erbium and thulium for Thule (Cleve 1879)

name: Ytterbium and Lutetium
description: The last rare earth found in nature, split from ytterbium (Urbain 1907)

name: Solar Cell
description: A silicon wafer turns sunlight straight into current (Bell Labs 1954)

name: Isotope Separation
description: Uranium-235 is 0.7% of uranium and chemically the same: only its lighter weight can part it (Oak Ridge 1945)

name: Nuclear Reactor
description: A pile of uranium and graphite went critical under a Chicago stand: neutrons split uranium faster than they escape (Fermi 1942)

name: Reprocessing
description: Behind lead glass, spent fuel is dissolved and its uranium and plutonium pulled out by solvent (PUREX, Savannah River 1954)

name: Neptunium
description: The first element beyond uranium, made by neutrons on uranium (McMillan and Abelson 1940)

name: Technetium
description: The gap at 43 was filled by an element no ore holds: first from a cyclotron part, now by the kilogram from fission (Perrier and Segre 1937)

name: Promethium
description: The missing rare earth, found among the fission products of the Oak Ridge reactor (Marinsky, Glendenin and Coryell 1945)

name: Americium and Curium
description: Plutonium soaked in neutrons gives americium, and americium gives curium (Seaborg, James, Morgan and Ghiorso 1944)

name: Cyclotron
description: Particles whirled in a magnet and kicked at every half turn reach millions of volts (Lawrence 1932): astatine was made in one (1940)

name: Berkelium and Californium
description: Alpha particles on americium and curium gave elements 97 and 98, named for Berkeley and California (1949-50)

name: Mendelevium
description: Einsteinium from the first hydrogen bomb's debris, bombarded in the cyclotron one atom at a time (Ghiorso 1955)

name: Superconducting Magnets
description: Niobium-titanium wire cooled by liquid helium carries current with no loss: the magnets of every big accelerator and MRI scanner

name: Integrated Circuit
description: A whole circuit printed on one chip of silicon (Kilby 1958, Noyce 1959): the start of the information age

name: Compound Semiconductors
description: Gallium arsenide gives off light where silicon cannot: the first visible LED and the semiconductor laser (Holonyak 1962). The Heavy-Ion Accelerator needs its wafers

name: Electromagnetic Isotope Separation
description: Lawrence's calutrons bent uranium ions apart by mass at Oak Ridge; today they make rare isotopes such as calcium-48

name: Heavy-Ion Accelerator
description: Whole nuclei, not just helium, fired at heavy targets: elements 102 and 103 at Berkeley and Dubna (1958-66)

name: Rutherfordium to Seaborgium
description: Carbon, nitrogen and oxygen beams on californium gave elements 104 to 106 (Ghiorso, Berkeley 1969-74)

name: Cold Fusion of Heavy Nuclei
description: Gentle collisions of medium nuclei with lead and bismuth gave elements 107 to 113, one atom a week (GSI 1981-96, RIKEN 2004)

name: Calcium-48 Hot Fusion
description: A calcium-48 beam on actinide targets reached the island of stability's shore: elements 114 to 118 (Oganessian, Dubna 1999-2010)

name: Neodymium Magnets
description: Neodymium, iron and boron make the strongest magnets (Sagawa 1984): direct-drive wind turbines with no gearbox

name: Composite Armour
description: Ceramic tiles shatter the bullet and woven aramid catches it: boron carbide plates over titanium (Kwolek's Kevlar 1965)

name: The Periodic Table Complete
description: IUPAC named the last four elements in 2016: the seventh row of the periodic table is full

name: Radioisotope Generator
description: Neptunium irradiated into plutonium-238, whose decay heat thermocouples turn into current for decades (Transit 4A 1961, Voyager 1977)

name: Smoke Detector
description: A speck of americium ionises the air in a chamber; smoke stops the current and the alarm sounds (Duane Pearsall 1965)

name: Lithium-Ion Battery
description: Lithium ions shuttle between a cobalt oxide cathode and a carbon anode (Goodenough 1980, Yoshino 1985, Sony 1991)

name: Optical Fibre
description: Light in glass fibre amplified by erbium carries a world network (Kao 1966, Payne and Desurvire 1987)

name: Element Analyzer
description: Curium-244 alpha particles and X-rays read every element in a rock: the APXS of the Mars rovers (Sojourner 1997)

name: Oil Refining
description: Retort oil shale in an alembic and distil the crude oil into naphtha, kerosene, diesel and bitumen (Young 1851, Drake 1859); bitumen binds asphalt roads

name: Diesel Engine
description: Diesel's compression-ignition engine turns a generator: current from oil with no boiler or water

name: Thermal Cracking
description: Burton's pressure stills crack heavy oil into gasoline; the cracked gas is rich in ethylene

name: Coal Liquefaction
description: Bergius hydrogenated powdered coal at 200 atmospheres into petrol and middle oil (Nobel Prize 1931)

name: Liquid-Fuel Rocket
description: Goddard flew a rocket on liquid fuel and liquid oxygen (1926): kerosene rockets push an elytra like three charges of gunpowder

name: PVC
description: Vinyl chloride from ethylene and chlorine, polymerised and made flexible by Semon (1926); PVC-sleeved cable carries current four times as far as bare wire

name: Polyethylene
description: ICI found that ethylene at 1500 atmospheres with a trace of oxygen becomes a waxy white solid (1933): first radar cable, then everything

name: Catalytic Reforming
description: Platforming: naphtha over platinum becomes high-octane gasoline, benzene and xylene, and gives up hydrogen (UOP 1949)

name: Nylon
description: Carothers' nylon 6-6 (DuPont 1935), the first fully synthetic fibre: stockings, rope and parachutes

name: Calutron Enrichment
description: The Y-12 calutrons enriched the uranium of the first bomb; afterwards they enriched lithium-6, boron-10 and hundreds of other isotopes for science

name: Heavy Water
description: Norsk Hydro's heavy water slows neutrons without catching them, so natural uranium can sustain a chain reaction (the Canadian CANDU reactors)

name: Boron Control Rods
description: Boron-10 swallows neutrons: control rods throttle a reactor so it stops burning fuel it has no room to store

name: Tritium
description: Lithium-6 in a reactor catches a neutron and splits into helium and tritium; tritium's soft beta light makes signs glow for decades with no power

name: Gas Compression
description: Seamless drawn steel cylinders hold gas at 150 atmospheres (Mannesmann 1885): a Compressor upgrade lets a machine fill them, nine flasks to a cylinder

name: Regenerative Furnace
description: Siemens passes the hot flue gas through brick checkerwork that then heats the incoming air: a Regenerator upgrade halves a fuel-fired machine's heat loss

name: Basic Refractories
description: Thomas and Gilchrist line the converter with burnt lime and dolomite that stand the heat and the slag: a Refractory Lining lets a fuel-fired machine run 150 °C hotter

name: By-Product Recovery
description: By-product coke ovens catch the gas instead of burning it off: a Gas Recovery Hood bottles the gases a machine vents

name: Electric Motor
description: Tesla's induction motor turns a paddle in the vessel: a Mechanical Stirrer makes a machine work 50% faster for a quarter more fuel or current

name: Catalyst Beds
description: Mittasch tests thousands of catalysts for Haber's ammonia: a Catalyst Bed doubles the rate of reactions over iron, nickel, platinum or vanadium oxide

name: Automatic Mill
description: Oliver Evans' mill moves grain from step to step with no hand on it: an Output Pusher moves a machine's products into the chest next to it

name: Gas Mains
description: Winsor and Clegg lit London with coal gas sent through iron mains from gasholders (1812): Fluid Pipes join machines to tanks, and Tank Plates build a tank as big as you like

name: Rendering
description: Simmer meat, fat and bone in a kettle: tallow for candles and soap, and protein meal for the animals

name: Oil Pressing
description: Squeeze seeds in a screw press for oil; the cake left over feeds cattle

name: Soap Boiling
description: Boil fat or oil with the potash of wood ash: soft soap, and glycerol in the liquor

name: Pit Tanning
description: Lay hides in pits of bark liquor for months: four pieces of flesh make one leather, slowly and without a crafting grid

name: Mashing
description: Malt turns the starch of grain and potatoes into sugar, and yeast the sugar into alcohol

name: Sweet Oil of Vitriol
description: Distil spirit with a little oil of vitriol: diethyl ether, a solvent and a fuel (Cordus)

name: Alum Making
description: Dissolve clay in oil of vitriol and add potash: alum crystals, which taw rabbit hide into leather (Marggraf)

name: Hard Soap
description: Soda ash or a handful of salt makes soap that sets in hard bars (Aleppo, Castile)

name: Gas Liquor
description: Wash the ammonia out of coke-oven gas and neutralise it with acid: sulfate of ammonia for the fields

name: Superphosphate
description: Dissolve bones or phosphate rock in sulfuric acid: the first factory fertilizer (Lawes)

name: Starch Sugar
description: Boil starch with a little acid and it becomes sugar, faster than malt (Kirchhoff)

name: Vulcanization
description: Tap latex from rubber trees in the jungle and cure the rubber with sulfur: tough, springy and waterproof (Goodyear)

name: Prussian Blue
description: Blood calcined with potash and struck with green vitriol: the first synthetic pigment, made in a Dye Vat (Diesbach)

name: Tar Distillation
description: Catch the tar of the coke oven and cut it in a still: benzene, carbolic acid, anthracene, and pitch for tarmac (Mansfield)

name: Nitrobenzene
description: Benzene stirred into nitric and sulfuric acid: oil of mirbane, the way to aniline (Mitscherlich)

name: Aniline
description: Reduce nitrobenzene with iron filings and a little acid: aniline, the base of the coal tar dyes (Bechamp)

name: Fuchsine
description: Aniline and arsenic acid give magenta, the dye that made the aniline fortunes (Verguin)

name: Picric Acid
description: Nitrate carbolic acid three times: a yellow silk dye, and later Lyddite

name: Alizarin
description: Madder red from anthracene in a pressure vessel: the end of the madder fields (Graebe, Liebermann, Caro)

name: Antiseptic Surgery
description: Carbolic acid on wounds, hands and instruments: carbolic soap cures an early Infection (Lister)

name: Anaesthesia
description: Ether on a cloth puts a patient to sleep: a cure for a zombie villager takes half as long (Morton)

name: Dynamite
description: Nitroglycerin soaked into diatomite is safe to handle: Mining Charges break a 5 by 5 by 5 block of rock and keep every block (Nobel)

name: Cordite
description: Nitroglycerin and guncotton in cords: Cordite Cartridges hit 25% harder from the Breech-Loading Rifle and make no smoke (Abel and Dewar)

name: Aspirin
description: Salicylic acid from phenol in the Autoclave, then acetylated: aspirin eases nausea and fatigue and cures an early Infection (Kolbe, Hoffmann)

name: Bordeaux Mixture
description: Copper vitriol and lime sprayed on vines stops mildew: sprayed crops never wash out or wilt in the dark, and berry bushes stop scratching (Millardet)

name: Insect Powder
description: Dried Dalmatian daisies ground to powder: an Insect Spray that kills spiders, silverfish and endermites (and bees)

name: Vacuum Distillation
description: A pump on a still lowers the boiling points: a Vacuum Pump makes a still, kettle or crystallizer work 100 °C cooler

name: Calcium Carbide
description: Quicklime and coke fused in the arc make carbide; water on carbide gives acetylene, the flame of the miner's Carbide Lamp (Willson 1892)

name: Nitrolime
description: Hot carbide takes up nitrogen: calcium cyanamide, the first fertilizer made from the air (Frank and Caro 1898)

name: Oxy-Acetylene Welding
description: Acetylene burnt in pure oxygen is hot enough to melt steel: a Welding Torch mends metal tools and armour with ingots and no experience (Fouche and Picard 1903)

name: Formaldehyde
description: Wood spirit and air over red-hot silver give formaldehyde, the other half of the first plastics (Hofmann 1867; made by the tonne from 1889)

name: Bakelite
description: Phenol and formaldehyde under pressure set into Bakelite: hard, dark, and it takes a polish; coloured Bakelite blocks and Bakelite-cased Geiger counters (Baekeland 1907)

name: Urea Synthesis
description: Ammonia and carbon dioxide at 150 atmospheres become urea, the richest nitrogen fertilizer (Bosch and Meiser 1922)

name: Prilled Fertilizer
description: Melt dropped down a tall tower freezes into hard round prills that flow and keep: ammonium nitrate, and NPK prills that make crops grow twice as fast

name: TNT
description: Toluene nitrated three times: TNT is safe to melt and pour, and a Demolition Charge breaks even obsidian (Wilbrand 1863; army filling from 1902)

name: Acetone Fermentation
description: Weizmann's bacterium turns the starch of grain or potatoes into acetone and butanol: the acetone for wartime cordite (1916)

name: Neoprene
description: Chloroprene rubber from acetylene: it shrugs off oil and cold; a neoprene Wetsuit swims like a dolphin and never freezes (Carothers 1931)

name: Buna Rubber
description: Synthetic rubber from alcohol and benzene, no jungle needed: Rubber Wheels, and a Conveyor Belt that empties a machine four items at a time (Lebedev 1926, IG Farben 1929)

name: Sulfa Drugs
description: A red dye cured streptococcus in mice; its active half, sulfanilamide, cures Infection and even sepsis (Domagk 1932, Trefouel 1935)

name: Biodiesel
description: Plant oil or tallow with methanol and lye gives methyl esters that run a Diesel Generator: fuel from the farm (Chavanne 1937)

name: Styrene and Polystyrene
description: Styrene joins into clear, light polystyrene; blown with gas it is foam: Foam Lagging for cool machines and Insulation that keeps ice from melting (Dow 1941)

name: Penicillin
description: Fleming's mould grown in deep, stirred tanks of sterile air: penicillin cures Infection, guards against it for 20 minutes, and with Weakness cures a zombie villager (1928, 1943)

name: Streptomycin
description: An antibiotic from a soil bacterium, the first to cure tuberculosis: it cures Infection and guards against it for 20 minutes (Schatz and Waksman 1943)

name: DDT
description: An insecticide that lasts: a DDT Duster leaves ground that kills insects for three days, and the chickens near it lay half as often (Muller 1939; Silent Spring 1962)

name: Weed Killer
description: A plant hormone that kills broad-leaved weeds and spares grass and grain: Weed Killer clears flowers, ferns, vines and leaves (1945)

name: Atrazine
description: Sprayed before anything grows: Pre-Emergent stops grass and mycelium spreading onto the ground for ten days (Geigy 1958)

name: Plastic Explosive
description: RDX from hexamine, kneaded with oil: a Shaped Charge with a copper liner bores a tunnel sixteen blocks deep (Henning 1898; Munroe effect)

name: ANFO
description: Fertilizer prills soaked in diesel: the cheapest blasting agent; an ANFO Charge breaks a 9x9x9 cube for the quarry (1955)

name: Radiation Countermeasures
description: Potassium iodide tablets keep radioiodine out of the body, and Prussian blue capsules bind radiocaesium: each cuts the dose from fission products for a day

name: Glyphosate
description: A weed killer that kills every green plant: Field Clear spares only crops grown from tolerant seeds (Franz 1970)

name: Recombinant DNA
description: Genes cut and pasted into bacteria: the Bioreactor, a chip-run vessel for engineered microbes (Cohen and Boyer 1973)

name: Cellulosic Ethanol
description: Enzymes break the cellulose of any plant to sugar: ethanol from logs, leaves and straw

name: Tolerant Seeds
description: A bacterial gene makes wheat shrug off glyphosate: Tolerant Seeds survive Field Clear and grow a tenth faster

name: PLA Bioplastic
description: Plastic fermented from sugar that composts away: flower pots and item frames from PLA

name: mRNA Vaccine
description: Messenger RNA in a droplet of fat teaches the body its enemy: seven game days with no Infection (Kariko and Weissman; 2020)

name: Amifostine
description: A radioprotector from the Walter Reed programme: for an hour, radiation does half the harm (1959; approved 1995)

name: Quarry Hammers
description: Quarrymen's sledges and navvies' broad shovels: a Sledgehammer breaks 3x3 of stone and an Excavator 3x3 of earth, slowly, at one wear per block

name: Rock Blasting
description: Black powder packed into a drilled hole (Schemnitz 1627): a Blasting Charge breaks a 3x3x3 block of stone, drops all of it and never harms a machine

name: Rock Drill
description: Compressed air drove the drills that cut the Mont Cenis tunnel (Sommeiller 1861; Ingersoll 1871): the Air Compressor fills cylinders and the Pneumatic Rock Drill mines one block, a 1x3 tunnel or 3x3

name: Lead-Acid Battery
description: Plante's lead plates in sulfuric acid store charge you can carry: a Lead-Acid Battery Pack holds 1,500 kJ and fills on a Charging Bench joined to the wire

name: Rotary Hammer
description: An electric motor turns and hammers the bit at once (Bosch 1932): the Rotary Hammer runs on a battery pack and never slows you

name: Chainsaw
description: A cutting chain driven round a bar (Stihl 1926): the Chainsaw fells a whole tree, up to 128 logs, on battery power

name: Heavy Mining Drill
description: Diamond core drilling: the Heavy Mining Drill adds a 5x5 head and a vein mode that follows one ore up to 32 blocks

name: Lithium-Ion Pack
description: Four times the charge of lead at half the weight: a Lithium-Ion Pack holds 6,000 kJ and the Heavy Mining Drill no longer slows you

name: Ore-Seeking Drill
description: The element analyzer built into the drill head: in vein mode, use the Heavy Mining Drill on an ore to read the whole vein before you dig

name: Surveying
description: Pace out the land and draw it on a tablet, as at Ga-Sur: the Field Atlas sketches what you walk past, with no coordinates

name: Magnetic Compass
description: A magnetised needle points north: the Atlas shows north, your exact place and facing, and a compass bar while you hold it

name: Quadrant and Astrolabe
description: Measure the height of the pole star and you know how far north you are: the Atlas shows Z, a scale bar, and draws twice as far

name: Portolan Charts
description: Sailors copied each other's coastlines: sneak and use the Atlas with paper in your other hand to make an Atlas Copy for someone else

name: Marine Chronometer
description: Harrison's H4 keeps time at sea, and the time difference gives longitude: the Atlas shows X as well

name: Hot-Air Balloon
description: The Montgolfiers' balloon lifts an observer above the land: a Survey Balloon draws 128 blocks all round at once

name: Triangulation and Theodolite
description: Ramsden's great theodolite measures angles to a fraction of a second: the Atlas draws sharp, with relief shading and contour lines every 8 blocks

name: Geological Map
description: William Smith coloured England by the rock beneath the soil: the Atlas gains a layer showing the bedrock under every column you walk past

name: Species Plantarum
description: Linnaeus counted stamens with a hand lens and gave every plant two Latin names: the Tree Compendium shows each tree's scientific name, family and native range

name: Geography of Plants
description: Humboldt carried a barometer and thermometer up Chimborazo and saw the forests change with height and heat: the Compendium shows each biome's climate

name: The Red List
description: The IUCN begins listing species at risk of extinction: the Compendium shows how threatened each tree is in the wild

name: Diamond Core Drill
description: Leschot's drill with a crown of diamonds brings up a whole core of rock: the Atlas gains an ore layer from your cores and the ores you mine

name: Mapping Radioactivity
description: The Curies hunted uranium minerals with an electroscope: every reading you take is marked on the Atlas's radiation layer

name: Magnetic and Seismic Prospecting
description: Magnetometers and the first seismic reflection surveys see ore bodies from the surface: an anomaly layer, without naming the ore

name: Geiger Survey
description: Carry a Geiger counter and the radiation where you walk is logged on the Atlas by itself

name: Radio Direction Finding
description: Radio beacons let ships and aircraft fix their place: a Radio Transmitter shares your Atlas markers with every player who knows radio within 512 blocks

name: Radar
description: Radio echoes off aircraft won the Battle of Britain: a Radar Station shows creatures and players within 96 blocks on the Atlas, and a Handheld Radar gives you a minimap

name: Airborne Gamma Spectrometry
description: A sodium iodide crystal tells the gamma rays of uranium, thorium and caesium apart: the Atlas splits radiation by isotope, and reads the ground from the air

name: Satellite and Tracking Station
description: Sputnik's beeps were heard all round the world: launch a satellite and a Tracking Station maps 512 blocks all round it each day, without going there

name: Multispectral Scanner
description: Landsat saw rocks and minerals in bands of light the eye cannot: your satellites note the rock and the ores near the surface of what they map

name: Global Positioning System
description: Atomic clocks in orbit give anyone their place to a few metres: a GPS Receiver shows the minimap anywhere, marks where you die and routes you to your markers

name: De re metallica
description: Agricola describes every ore and how miners find it: the Mineral Compendium shows each ore's mineral and the depths where it is found

name: Theory of the Earth
description: Hutton reads at Siccar Point that rocks are made, worn away and made again: the Compendium sorts rocks into igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic and names the formation underfoot

name: Thin Sections
description: Sorby grinds rock to slices thin enough to see through under a microscope: the Compendium shows the minerals each rock is made of

name: X-ray Diffraction
description: The Braggs bounce X-rays off crystals and read the spacing of their atoms: the Compendium shows each mineral's formula and crystal system

name: Heated Greenhouse
description: Glass houses warmed by a stove (Chelsea Physic Garden 1681): tropical and desert plants grow far from home

name: Cold Greenhouse
description: Linde's refrigerating machine (1876) keeps a glasshouse cold: arctic and alpine plants grow anywhere; ice will do while it lasts

name: Alkaloids
description: Pelletier and Caventou drew emetine and quinine out of plants with acid water; Runge found caffeine (1819)

name: Food Antioxidants
description: Fat kept from going rancid with a pinch of NDGA from the creosote bush (1943), until safer antioxidants replaced it

name: Vitamins
description: Szent-Györgyi drew hexuronic acid out of paprika (1928): vitamin C, the cure for scurvy, and with the same methods arbutin from bearberry

name: Domestication
description: Keep the seeds of the best plants: the Seed Lens shows what traits a seed or a crop has

name: Animal Husbandry
description: Pen the herd and feed it: a Feeding Trough feeds the animals around it so they breed and grow

name: Crop Rotation
description: Three-field rotation: soybeans, beans, indigo and alfalfa leave the ground fertilized when harvested

name: Natural Dyes
description: Blue from indigo, red from madder root: the Dye Vat dyes with plants

name: Plant Hybridization
description: Kölreuter crossed tobacco plants by hand: the Pollination Brush chooses the father of a plant's seeds

name: Tobacco Wash
description: Tobacco steeped in water kills caterpillars on crops: the first insecticide of the farm

name: Mendel's Laws
description: Mendel counted his peas: each trait is two factors, one from each parent. The Seed Lens shows the genes themselves

name: Silage
description: Goffart packed green maize in a pit and it kept all winter: the Silo turns maize, sorghum and alfalfa into silage

name: Nitrogen Fixation
description: Hellriegel and Wilfarth show that bacteria in the root nodules of legumes take nitrogen from the air: Inoculant gives a legume its rhizobia

name: Hybrid Maize
description: Shull and Jones cross inbred lines of maize: the first generation grows with hybrid vigour. The Seed Lens marks hybrids and pure lines

name: Balanced Feed
description: Feed with energy, protein, minerals and salt in the right shares: animals grow and breed faster on it

name: X-ray Mutagenesis
description: Stadler X-rays barley seeds and the plants come out changed: the Seed Irradiator makes mutations twenty times as common

name: DNA Double Helix
description: Franklin's X-ray picture, Watson and Crick's model: genes are written in DNA. The Seed Lens shows every trait, and the stature gene of wheat and rice

name: Gamma Garden
description: A cobalt-60 source in a field of crops (Japan 1960): seeds of the plants around it mutate twenty times as often

name: DNA Sequencing
description: Sanger reads DNA letter by letter: the DNA Sequencer shows the whole genome of a seed

name: PCR
description: Mullis copies a stretch of DNA a billion times by heating and cooling it: the Thermocycler tests seeds for a marker's genes and sorts them

name: Transgenesis
description: Sanford shoots gold beads coated with DNA into plant cells: the Gene Gun gives crops the Bt, EPSPS, golden rice and DREB genes

name: CRISPR
description: Charpentier and Doudna turn a bacterial defence into scissors for DNA: the CRISPR Kit rewrites one gene of a crop

name: Rubber Belt Conveyor
description: Thomas Robins' rubber-covered belt carries coal and ore for miles (1891): the faster Rubber Belt, the Steel Hopper to keep up with it, and the Belt Sorter that turns chosen items aside

name: Moving Assembly Line
description: Ford's line brings the work to the worker on rollers and chains (1913): the Roller Conveyor and the Stainless Steel Hopper

name: Hide Tent
description: Hides on a frame of poles: a Tent you sleep in far from home, which never moves your spawn point

name: Leather Backpack
description: A leather bag on two straps: a Leather Backpack with 27 places that picks up the plant and mineral specimens you walk over

name: Hunting Nets
description: A knotted net thrown over game: the Rope Net catches a small animal alive and lets it out where you throw it

name: Explorer's Compass
description: Bearings and travellers' accounts: choose a biome and the Explorer's Compass points to the nearest one

name: Animal Cage
description: The menageries' travelling cages: the Steel Cage carries any animal, a horse or a cow too, and never wears out

name: Electric Cap Lamp
description: Edison's miner's lamp: a tungsten bulb on the helmet fed by the battery pack, light 15 that follows you

name: Sodium Street Lighting
description: Low-pressure sodium vapour shines yellow at 589 nm: a Sodium Lamp on a post keeps monsters from spawning within 24 blocks

name: Night Vision
description: A silver-oxygen-caesium photocathode turns faint infrared into a picture: Night Vision Goggles show the dark and outline monsters

name: Nylon Backpack
description: Light, tough nylon on an aluminium frame: a Nylon Backpack with 54 places

name: White LED
description: Blue gallium nitride light (Nakamura 1993) under a yellow phosphor gives white: LED Lamps reach 40 blocks on little power, and the LED Spotlight Helmet lights where you look

name: Sericulture
description: Silkworms fed on white mulberry leaves spin cocoons; boiled, each gives one long silk thread (Leizu, China)

name: Carmine
description: The Aztecs' crimson of dried cochineal, shipped to Europe by Spain: dye red in a Dye Vat with cochineal

name: Shellac
description: Sticklac scraped from Indian trees, washed and melted: shellac, varnish for furniture and the insulation of early electricity

name: On the Origin of Species
description: Darwin's finches and pigeons: species change by natural selection. The Animal Compendium tells each animal's story

name: Antivenom
description: Calmette raises horse serum against snake venom: venom, salt and a bottle make Antivenom, which cures poison

name: Hirudin
description: The anticoagulant of the medicinal leech, drawn out in a Digestion Vat

name: Exenatide
description: A peptide from Gila monster saliva becomes a diabetes medicine, made in the Bioreactor

name: Guano
description: Peruvian seabird guano, leached with hot water and potash: saltpetre for powder and fields (the Guano Age, 1840-1880)

name: Galalith
description: Casein from skim milk hardened in formalin: galalith, the milk-stone of buttons and pens (Spitteler and Krische 1897)

name: Tyrian Purple
description: The Phoenicians' purple from murex snails, worth more than gold: dye purple in a Dye Vat with murex

name: Vitamin D
description: Cod and shark liver oil cures rickets (McCollum 1922): vitamin D3 drawn out in a Digestion Vat

name: Chitosan
description: Crab shells boiled in strong lye lose their acetyl groups: chitosan, for wound dressings and water filters (Rouget 1859)

name: LAL Test
description: Horseshoe crab blood clots at a trace of bacterial endotoxin: every injectable medicine is tested with it (Bang and Levin)

name: Green Fluorescent Protein
description: The glow of the crystal jelly made by bacteria: GFP, a living marker for cells (Shimomura 1962, Chalfie 1994)
